To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a moderate inspiratory load elicits consistent activation of discrete brain regions in healthy humans, and that the temporal characteristics of the fMRI responses suggest the presence of habituation and/or respiratory afterdischarge mechanisms.
the human brain regions mediating compensatory responses to resistive loading include the pons, inter peduncular nucleus, and basal forebrain.

a moderate inspiratory resistive load is associated with regional activation of discrete human brain locations; certain brain regions have been previously implicated in mediation of load breathing in animal models; and temporal changes in fMR signal may indicate respiratory habituation phenomena.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of human brain sites meditating compensatory ventilatory responses.
identifying human brain regions underlying respiratory motor control and regulation.
the identification of human brain areas mediating responses to resistive breathing loads and with the temporal characteristics of these responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

fMRI signal increases in certain regions of the human brain during resistive loading are consistent with a central respiratory drive mechanism, and that these brain regions may play a role in ventilatory compensation to resistive loading.
the human brain regions identified by fMRI during resistive loading of the inspiratory muscles are likely to be involved in the control of loaded breathing.

the human brain regions underlying compensatory responses to resistive loading are not known, but that they are located in the ventral and/or dorsal pons, the interpeduncular nuclei, the basal forebrain, the putamen, and the cerebellum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fMRI signal increases in the human brain during resistive inspiratory loadings.
we identified specific brain sites that are involved in compensatory ventilatory responses in humans.
we have been able to identify brain regions involved in compensating for resistive inspiratory load in healthy humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain regions identified in our study are likely to be involved in respiratory control and could be the target for future studies of the pathophysiology of breathing disorders.
the fMRI approach is a useful tool for investigating human brain sites underlying breathing regulation.
fMRI can be used to map brain sites involved in respiratory regulation and to study the temporal characteristics of these sites in response to a variety of respiratory perturbations.
